title: Given a begin word, an end word, and a dictionary of equal-length words, find the length of the shortest transformation sequence that changes one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in the dictionary. Explain the breadth-first search solution, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Word Ladder (Shortest Transformation Chain One Letter at a Time)
keyPoints: Each word is a node in an implicit graph, and an edge connects two words that differ by exactly one letter.
BFS from the begin word finds the shortest transformation sequence because all edges have unit cost.
Neighbours are generated on the fly by trying every single-letter substitution and keeping only dictionary words.
A hash set for the dictionary gives O(1) membership checks; removing visited words doubles as a visited marker.
Time complexity is O(N * L * 26) where N is the dictionary size and L is the word length.
Bidirectional BFS from both ends can dramatically reduce the explored frontier for large dictionaries.

s1_definition.oneliner: Treat each word as a node in an implicit graph where one-letter changes are edges, then BFS from the begin word gives the shortest valid chain to the end word.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Implicit graph** – each word is a node; an edge connects two words that differ by exactly one letter.
- **BFS** – breadth-first search from the begin word finds the shortest path because all edges have unit cost.
- **On-the-fly neighbours** – for each word, try every single-letter substitution (L positions * 26 letters) and keep only dictionary words.
- **Hash set dictionary** – O(1) membership checks; removing a word from the set when it is enqueued prevents revisiting.
- **Bidirectional BFS** – searching from both the begin and end words simultaneously can dramatically shrink the explored frontier.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India migrates an old product code to a new one, but compliance forces every intermediate code to be a valid registered code in the catalogue, changing one character at a time. The bank wants the shortest valid chain from the old code to the new one.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Word Ladder BFS
================

Begin: "hit"   End: "cog"
Dict: {hot, dot, dog, lot, log, cog}

Level 1: ["hit"]                          steps=1
  Generate neighbours of "hit":
    h→a..z: ait,bit,...,hot(in dict!),...
    i→a..z: hat,hbt,...
    t→a..z: hia,hib,...
  Enqueue: "hot", remove from dict

Level 2: ["hot"]                          steps=2
  Neighbours: "dot"(dict), "lot"(dict), "hog"(not), ...
  Enqueue: "dot", "lot"

Level 3: ["dot", "lot"]                   steps=3
  "dot" → "dog"(dict)
  "lot" → "log"(dict)
  Enqueue: "dog", "log"

Level 4: ["dog", "log"]                   steps=4
  "dog" → "cog"(end word!) → return 5

Path: hit → hot → dot → dog → cog (5 words, 4 changes)


Bidirectional BFS
==================

  Front (from begin):  {hit}
  Back  (from end):    {cog}

  Expand front: hit → {hot}
  Expand back:  cog → {dog, log, cog→...}
  Expand front: hot → {dot, lot}
  Expand back:  {dog,log} → {dot(in front!)} → MEET!

  Frontier sizes are much smaller → faster

  Unidirectional:  explores ~26^d nodes
  Bidirectional:   explores ~2*26^(d/2) nodes
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Ladder is a shortest path problem hiding behind a string puzzle. Each word is a node in an implicit graph, and an edge connects any two words that differ by exactly one letter. Because all edges have unit cost, BFS from the begin word finds the shortest transformation sequence to the end word. Neighbours are generated on the fly by trying every single-letter substitution and checking against the dictionary.

The two implementation details that make this efficient are a hash set for the dictionary (O(1) membership checks) and removing each word from the set when it is enqueued (doubling as a visited marker). Processing the queue level by level and incrementing the step count after each level gives the shortest chain length the first time the end word is reached.

At the National Bank of India, the product team used this for product-code migration where compliance required every intermediate code to be valid in the catalogue and only one character could change per step. They loaded the catalogue into a hash set and ran level-by-level BFS to find the shortest compliant migration path.

For large dictionaries, bidirectional BFS searching from both the begin and end words simultaneously and meeting in the middle dramatically reduces the explored frontier. This is the key optimization that makes the algorithm practical at scale.

Remember one sentence: each word is a node, one-letter changes are edges, BFS gives the shortest chain, and removing words from the dictionary set prevents revisiting.
